newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq asks UN chief to help speed oil deal delivery.
newsitem.headline: Iraq asks UN chief to help speed oil deal delivery.

text.p: Iraqi Ambassador Nizar Hamdoon personally complained to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan Friday on the sluggish pace of food distribution under the oil-for-food deal, blaming the United States for increasingly blocking humanitarian contracts.

"We complained with the Secretary-General on the slowness of the process that not enough quantities have been accumulated to ensure the continuation of the distribution of the basic items of the Iraqi food basket," Hamdoon said.

At issue was the oil-for-food deal, which began Dec. 10 and allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of crude over six months, mainly to buy food and medicine for civilians suffering from sanctions imposed in 1990 after Baghdad troops invaded Kuwait.

Hamdoon said most "observers" were linking American blocks on contracts to U.S. disapproval of recent air flights by Iraq to ferry pilgrims to Mecca, a so-called "technical" violation of international restrictions.

"We don't make such linkeage because it is unacceptable to link any other event to this humanitarian package. But this is what most observers are doing, linking the American position on those contracts with that event, which obviously the Security Council dealt with in a smooth way, which has maybe made the Americans upset by the outcome," Hamdoon said.
"We appealed to him (Annan) to try and deal with the matter because it is his responsibility to overseee the implementation of the process," Hamdoon said.
On Thursday, following a U.N. sanctions committee meeting, the panel spokeswoman said for the first time seven humanitarian contracts were blocked.
Blocked contracts were for rice from Vietnam, beans from Sudan, and plastic bags, cooking oil, detergent, sugar and soap from Jordan. No reasons were given for the blocks.

As of Thursday, out of a total 498 humanitarian contracts submitted to the United Nations, 217 were received by the sanctions panel, and 122 had been approved. The others were either on hold, pending or blocked.
Hamdoon said Annan agreed to look into the matter.
"He agreed with us that something must be done to ensure the process goes smoothly and that enough quanities of those items are provided," Hamdoon said.
The U.N. would only say that Annan "discussed the means of ensuring implementation of Resolution 986 (oil-for-food)."
Hamdoon also said he suggested that Annan look into raising the number of staff processing humanitarian contracts from the current three to five or six.
The U.N. also would not comment on Hamdoon's suggestion that Annan meet with the sanctions committee, and the U.S. delegation over the blocked humanitarian contracts.

Also on Thursday, the sanctions committee announced it had blocked a number of contracts for Iraq deemed as "non-essential products." The blocks occurred under the broader purvey of the sanctions committee under Resolution 661, the basis for the trade ban on Iraq.
Hamdoon said the rejected contracts for marble, whisky glasses and jeans from Turkey were not associated with the oil-for-food deal, or Baghdad's quest for swifter humanitarian food distribution.
"That has nothing to do with 986, all other private business has to do with private sectors in Iraq which usually goes for contracts of different natures," Hamdoon said.
